strengths: The core idea is novel and well-motivated: replacing arbitrary artificial graph augmentations with biologically meaningful perturbations (gene knockdown teacher GRNs from LINCS) as supervision for GCL is a sensible and original contribution for biological network representation learning.

The unified probabilistic formulation is clean: expressing GCL via KL divergence (Eqs. 1–3) and deriving the supervised augmentation distribution (Eq. 6) provides a coherent framework, with Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 clarifying the relationship to conventional GCL.

Empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive: three cancer types from real TCGA patient data, 13 downstream tasks spanning node-level (GO/OncoKB annotations) and graph-level (Cox hazard, PAM50 subtype) tasks, multiple metrics (accuracy, macro F1, Jaccard, C-index), embedding-dimension ablation, PCA collapse analysis, and detailed dataset/preprocessing documentation in the appendix (including GRN estimation statistics and compute costs).

Honest treatment of limitations: the authors explicitly acknowledge that statistical superiority was not achieved in every task and that teacher GRNs were only validated for same-cancer-type knockdowns; future work directions are clearly stated.
Extensive reproducibility detail: hyperparameter search spaces and tuned values, optimizer, hardware, computation times, dataset versions and accessions are all reported.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is oversold. Theorem 1 is a direct application of the chain-rule decomposition of KL divergence, and Corollary 1 is a simple limiting argument; neither constitutes a substantial 'theoretical extension of GCL' as claimed. The paper would be better served by framing these as a unified formulation rather than theory.

A potentially confounded empirical comparison: SupGCL consumes additional supervision data (teacher GRNs from knockdown experiments) that no baseline has access to. There is no ablation or baseline variant that also uses the LINCS teacher networks (e.g., fine-tuning GRACE with the teacher data, or a distillation baseline), so it is unclear whether gains come from the proposed contrastive formulation or simply from extra data.

Reported improvements are modest and often within one standard deviation (e.g., BP breast 0.243±0.052 vs. w/o-pretrain 0.232±0.031; several node-level results in Tables 10–11 are not best), and no statistical significance tests are provided despite 10-fold/10-seed protocols. The claim of 'consistently outperformed' is therefore weakly supported.

Missing ablation on the key methodological knob τa. The theory claims that as τa→∞ SupGCL reduces to conventional GCL; an empirical sweep over τa verifying this continuum (and the accuracy–biological-faithfulness tradeoff described in Section 4) is absent, leaving the central theoretical claim empirically unverified. The tuned value is 0.25 for all settings, suggesting the search may not have explored this axis meaningfully.

A significant distribution shift between teacher GRNs (cancer cell lines MCF7/A549/HT29) and patient GRNs (TCGA) is acknowledged only as a limitation; no experiment probes sensitivity to this gap (e.g., cross-cancer-type teachers, cell-line-only pretraining), which is central to the method's premise.

Reproducibility gaps: the sentence 'Our implementation and all experimental codes are available on' is truncated with no URL or repository reference; GRN construction relies on a specific supercomputer (Fugaku) and INGOR pipeline that external researchers cannot easily replicate, and the induced variance of the estimated networks is not propagated into the downstream evaluation.

Presentation issues: typos and incomplete sentences (e.g., the code availability sentence), the Graph Transformer is cited via the arXiv version of GPS, and some claims in Section 5.2 ('significantly higher performance') contradict the later admission that statistical significance was not established.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting and biologically motivated: using real gene knockdown experiments (LINCS) as teacher signal for graph contrastive learning on patient-specific GRNs is a novel and sensible way to make augmentation biologically faithful.

The paper provides a unified probabilistic formulation (Eq. 6-8) connecting augmentation-level and node-level contrastive losses via KL divergence, with Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 clarifying the relationship to conventional GCL (recovered as τa→∞).

Empirical effort is substantial: three cancer types, 13 downstream tasks across node- and graph-level, multiple evaluation metrics (subset accuracy, Macro F1, Jaccard, C-index), embedding-dimension ablations, PCA analysis of latent collapse, and public datasets (TCGA, LINCS) with detailed preprocessing documented in appendices.

Honest reporting: the authors acknowledge that SupGCL did not achieve statistically significant superiority in every task and clearly state the limitation that teacher GRNs come from the same cancer type.
Code and detailed computational environment are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The empirical gains are small and frequently within one standard deviation of baselines (e.g., Table 2: BP Breast 0.243 vs 0.232 w/o-pretrain; several CC and Rel. entries). The paper concedes that no task shows statistically significant superiority, yet the abstract and conclusion claim SupGCL 'achieves better performance than state-of-the-art baselines' and 'consistently outperformed existing GCL methods.' No statistical significance tests, effect sizes, or confidence intervals are reported, so the central claim is not adequately supported.

Potential data leakage in the evaluation protocol: Section 5.2 states pre-training was conducted on patient-specific GRNs from TCGA, and downstream evaluation used 10-fold cross-validation across patients. It is not stated whether test-fold patients' GRNs were excluded from pre-training. If the encoder saw all patients' graphs (including their survival/subtype-bearing expression profiles) during pre-training, graph-level task results may be inflated relative to baselines that pre-train on the same data—this needs explicit clarification.

The theoretical contribution is thin. Theorem 1 is a direct application of the standard KL chain-rule decomposition, and Corollary 1 (τa→∞ recovers uniform sampling) is a near-trivial limit. Framing this as 'theoretically demonstrating existing GCL methods are special cases' overstates the contribution; the independence assumption p(i,j,a,b)=p(i,j)pϕ(a,b) is doing most of the work and its consequences are not analyzed.

The proposed augmentation-level loss has both pϕ and qϕ parameterized by the same GNN fϕ; the paper identifies the trivial-solution risk but the proposed remedy (combining with node-level loss) is heuristic. There is no ablation isolating the contribution of the augmentation-level loss (LossAug) versus simply using knockdown-derived augmentation pairs, nor an analysis of sensitivity to τa, which the theory highlights as the key control knob.

Teacher GRNs come from a single cell line per cancer type (MCF7, A549, HT29 at 96h), which is a substantial domain mismatch with patient tumor GRNs; the effect of this mismatch and of the simple zero-masking knockdown simulation (zeroing node and edge features) is not studied. Confounded baselines: GraphCL performs poorly (apparent latent collapse), making the comparison field weak.

Presentation issues: an incomplete sentence ('Our implementation and all experimental codes are available on' — the URL is missing), a broken figure caption on page 3 for Figure 1's loss equation, and node-level t-SNE plots showing no label clustering for any method, which weakly supports the qualitative claims.

The claimed novelty relative to supervised augmentation ideas is modest: replacing random augmentations with experimentally derived perturbations is a targeted but incremental design change, and the paper does not compare against simpler supervised alternatives (e.g., training with knockdown-induced expression profiles directly, or a supervised auxiliary loss).

strengths: The core idea is original and biologically well-motivated: using real gene knockdown perturbation data (LINCS) as teacher signals for contrastive augmentation of patient-specific GRNs (TCGA), rather than generic artificial perturbations. This is a natural but previously under-explored direction for GCL on biological networks.

The probabilistic formulation is clean and unifying: Theorem 1 shows the proposed loss decomposes into a node-level GCL term weighted by a supervised augmentation distribution plus an augmentation-level term, and Corollary 1 shows conventional GCL is recovered as the temperature tau_a -> infinity. This gives a principled connection between supervised and standard GCL.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for an applied graph learning paper: three cancer types, 13 downstream tasks spanning node-level and graph-level, multiple metrics (subset accuracy, macro F1, Jaccard, C-index), embedding-dimension ablations, latent-space analysis including a collapse diagnosis (PCA explained variance), and reported computation times on identical architecture (5-layer Graph Transformer) for all methods.

Reproducibility-supporting details are extensive: full GRN estimation pipeline (INGOR/SiGN-BN, sampling runs, thresholds, supercomputer settings), dataset extraction details (TCGA cohorts, LINCS GSE92742, GO/OncoKB labeling), and hyperparameter search spaces and tuned values.
The paper is honest about its limitations (same-cancer-type teacher GRNs only; non-significant superiority in every single task), which is appreciated.
weaknesses: The empirical gains over strong baselines are modest and frequently within one standard deviation (e.g., BP Breast 0.243 vs 0.232 w/o-pretrain; Hazard Breast 0.650 vs 0.642 GRACE). No statistical significance testing is reported, yet the abstract and conclusion claim SupGCL 'consistently outperforms' and 'achieves significantly higher performance' - these central claims are not fully supported by the evidence. Appendix results also show SupGCL is not best on several macro F1/Jaccard entries, weakening the consistency claim.

The theoretical contribution is lightweight: Theorem 1 is a direct application of the standard KL chain-rule decomposition, and Corollary 1 follows from softmax saturation. Neither provides insight into when or why supervised augmentation should help; the 'special case' result is more of a consistency check than a theory.

The augmentation model itself is crude: a knockdown is simulated by simply zeroing the target gene's node feature and incident edge features, which may not reflect the actual downstream expression changes observed in knockdown experiments. No ablation compares this masking against alternative perturbation encodings, and no ablation isolates the contribution of Loss_Aug alone or the sensitivity to tau_a.

A significant domain gap exists between teacher GRNs (cancer cell lines MCF7/A549/HT29) and target GRNs (patient tumors), but the paper does not analyze or quantify how well cell-line-derived perturbation signals transfer to patients; this is arguably the crux of the method's premise.

There are ambiguity and potential data-handling concerns: how multiple knockdown experiments per gene are aggregated into a single teacher GRN is not clearly specified; and pre-training appears to use all patient GRNs before downstream 10-fold cross-validation, so the relationship between pre-training data and test folds (possible leakage of unlabeled test patient graphs, or worse) should be explicitly clarified.

Completeness/polish issues: the sentence 'Our implementation and all experimental codes are available on' is truncated with no link, which is a reproducibility concern; the abstract's '13 downstream tasks' accounting is only inferable across tables; the t-SNE node-level analysis concedes no label clustering is observed, limiting the interpretability payoff.

The GRN estimation step requires ~1,000 sampling runs on the Fugaku supercomputer (hundreds of node-hours), and the entire pipeline depends on this expensive, specific estimation software, which limits practical reproducibility and portability.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: rather than treating augmentation-induced structural changes as a nuisance (as in augmentation-free GCL), the paper exploits real gene knockdown experiments (LINCS) as supervisory signals for contrastive learning on GRNs. This reframing is original within the GCL literature and biologically sensible.

Clean probabilistic formulation: the method is cast as a KL-divergence contrastive objective with a supervised reference distribution over augmentations, and Theorem 1/Corollary 1 show conventional GCL is recovered as a special case (τa→∞), unifying artificial and biological augmentations.

Unusually comprehensive evaluation for this domain: 13 downstream tasks across three cancer types (node-, edge-, and graph-level), comparison with five baselines plus augmentation-correction/free methods (GCA, AFGRL, SimGRACE) and GCLink in the appendix, ablation on τa, embedding-dimension sweep, cross-domain pre-training/fine-tuning/OOD analysis, robustness to supervision-sample size and GRN-estimation noise, and GO/KEGG enrichment analysis of the latent space.

Honest reporting: the authors explicitly state that statistical significance was not achieved in every task, provide Bonferroni-corrected tests (Table 15), and candidly discuss the limitation that models do not transfer across cancer types (Section 6, Appendix G).

Strong reproducibility: full pipeline documentation (TCGA/LINCS extraction, Bayesian-network GRN estimation with INGOR/SiGN-BN on Fugaku, hyperparameter tables, compute times, seeds, cross-validation protocol) makes the study unusually reproducible for a biomedical ML paper.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'consistent' and 'significantly higher' superiority is overstated. Most gains over the strongest baseline (GRACE) are within one standard deviation (e.g., Hazard 0.650±0.059 vs 0.642±0.064; Subtype 0.847±0.036 vs 0.841±0.026), and the paper's own significance tests (Table 15) find only 4 significant differences—all against GraphCL/SGRL, none against GRACE, which is essentially the unsupervised ablation of the method.

The theoretical contribution is thin. Theorem 1 is a direct application of the standard KL chain-rule decomposition, and Corollary 1 is a trivial temperature limit; presenting these as a 'theoretical extension of GCL' oversells the novelty of the math.

The notion of 'real biological perturbation' is weaker than advertised. Teacher GRNs H_a are themselves computationally estimated Bayesian networks from LINCS knockdown expression data (via the same estimation pipeline as patient GRNs), and the artificial augmentation G_a models knockdown simply by zeroing node/edge features. The paper does not probe how sensitive the method is to errors in this two-layer estimation/simulation chain, nor how well the zero-feature knockdown simulation actually reflects the measured perturbation.

Node-level task design is coarse and results are modest: BP/CC tasks use only 3–4 hand-picked GO categories with subset accuracy around 0.24–0.29 (barely above w/o-pretrain), and the cancer-relevance task shows only a few points of accuracy gain (~0.60 vs ~0.57). Practical utility of the learned representations is not yet compelling.

Some internal inconsistencies and sensitivity issues: τa=0.10 is best for Hazard but the default is 0.25 (Table 4); the 3% edge threshold outperforms the default 5% (Table 21); Table 4's framing that SupGCL 'outperforms GRACE in all settings' conflicts with overlapping confidence intervals. Cross-domain results (Appendix G) also reveal that fine-tuned models fail badly OOD (C-index 0.583–0.603), limiting the claimed generality.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: confusing assumption notation in Theorem 1, a jump from Eq. (7) to Eq. (8) whose justification is compressed, typos ('contractive learning scheme', 'contractive' loss), and importance-sampling steps in Algorithm 1 that are hard to verify without the derivation.

Significance beyond the specific setting is unclear: the method relies on paired patient GRNs and matched cell-line knockdown GRNs restricted to 975 landmark genes and three cancer types; whether the supervised-augmentation idea transfers to other graph domains or larger gene sets remains untested.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting: using perturbational data from real knockdown experiments (LINCS) as supervision for graph contrastive learning on patient-specific GRNs (TCGA), framing augmentation-induced structural change as information rather than a nuisance. This inverts a current trend (augmentation-free GCL) in a way that is conceptually appealing for the biology domain.

The empirical evaluation is broad: 13 downstream tasks across three cancer types, five-plus baselines (GAE, GraphCL, GRACE, SGRL, plus GCA/AFGRL/SimGRACE and a GCLink variant in the appendix), ablation over the augmentation temperature, embedding-dimension analysis, cross-cancer-type training, robustness to sample size and GRN-estimation noise, and a GO/KEGG enrichment analysis of the latent space.

Honest limitations discussion: the authors acknowledge lack of statistical significance on individual tasks, the failure of fine-tuned models to transfer across cancer types, and the caveat that the τa ablation is not strictly identical to GRACE.
The paper is generally well-organized, with substantial appendices covering data construction, hyperparameters, and computation time.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim ('consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines' across all 13 tasks) is overstated. Improvements over the strongest baselines (GRACE, SGRL) are typically within one standard deviation, and the authors' own significance testing (Table 15) finds only four Bonferroni-corrected significant differences—three of them against GraphCL, the weakest baseline. The paper is not the 'new SOTA' the abstract implies; it is a consistent but marginal improvement.

The 'supervision' is weaker than advertised. The teacher GRNs H_a are not measured perturbation networks; they are themselves computationally estimated Bayesian networks from cell-line knockdown expression data. Thus the method matches one estimate (artificial feature-zeroing augmentation of a patient GRN) against another estimate (LINCS-derived network), introducing a serious confound: differences between TCGA and LINCS network estimates (different sample sizes, tissue context, estimation noise) may drive apparent gains rather than 'biologically faithful' perturbation information. No experiment isolates this (e.g., a baseline that simply pretrains on the union of patient and knockdown GRNs without the augmentation-level loss, or using shuffled/mismatched teacher graphs).

Moreover, the artificial augmentation—zeroing a node's features and incident edges—is essentially the same feature-masking perturbation the paper criticizes as biologically implausible, which undercuts the framing that biological structural changes are being faithfully incorporated.

The theoretical contribution is shallow. Theorem 1 is a direct application of the KL chain rule, and Corollary 1 (τa → ∞ recovers node-level GCL) is a trivial limit. The independence assumption p(i,j,a,b) = p(i,j)p(a,b) is asserted without biological or statistical justification. Claiming this as a 'theoretical extension of GCL' in the contributions list overstates its depth.

The ablation in Table 4 does not cleanly support the theory: performance is non-monotone in τa, the default (0.25) is not the best setting for Hazard, and the claimed convergence toward GRACE is noisy; the authors themselves note the comparison to GRACE is 'not strictly identical,' which weakens the empirical validation of Corollary 1.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and the pipeline depends on proprietary-scale computation (GRN estimation on the Fugaku supercomputer, 21+ GPU-hours per model per cancer type), making independent verification difficult.

Potential evaluation concern: pre-training appears to use all patient GRNs before the 10-fold cross-validated fine-tuning. Whether pre-training saw test patients' graphs (a transductive setting) is not clarified; if so, this should be stated and its implications discussed.

There is no obvious ablation isolating the contribution of the augmentation-level supervised loss beyond the τa sweep, and the improvement in enrichment/cluster analysis (Appendix I) over GAE is qualitative rather than quantitative.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('contractive learning'), a partially garbled Figure 1 label, and node-level subset accuracies around 0.24 for 3-label tasks suggest the downstream tasks themselves may be poorly calibrated, making small deltas hard to interpret.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting and well-motivated: instead of treating augmentation-induced structural changes as noise (the augmentation-free trend), SupGCL exploits real perturbation data from LINCS knockdown experiments as supervisory signal for GCL on GRNs. This is a conceptually novel reframing within the GCL literature.

The probabilistic formulation is clean and provides a unifying view: Theorem 1 decomposes the supervised loss into a node-level GCL term re-weighted by the supervised augmentation distribution plus an augmentation-level KL term, and Corollary 1 shows conventional unsupervised GCL is recovered as τa → ∞. This connects the method to prior work rigorously, if modestly.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: 13 tasks across three cancer types, node-, graph-, and edge-level downstream tasks, multiple metrics beyond headline accuracy (Macro F1, Jaccard, C-index), ablation on the augmentation temperature, latent-space collapse analysis (PCA), link-prediction comparison including a GCLink-style variant, and cross-domain pre-training/fine-tuning/OOD experiments.

Robustness analyses (patient sample size, supervision sample size down to ~2 experiments/gene, GRN-estimation filtering thresholds) and full hyperparameter/compute documentation strengthen reproducibility of the reported experiments.

The paper is honest about limitations: it explicitly reports that most pairwise comparisons are not statistically significant (Appendix F.4), that the τa experiment and GRACE are not strictly identical, and that cross-cancer-type generalization fails at fine-tuning; this candor is commendable and the biological enrichment analysis (GO/KEGG) adds domain credibility.
Dense, carefully documented datasets (TCGA, LINCS GSE92742) with explicit filtering rules and statistics support replication of the data pipeline.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin relative to its billing. Theorem 1 is a direct application of the standard KL chain-rule decomposition, and Corollary 1 follows trivially from softmax saturation. The claim of 'theoretically demonstrating that existing GCL methods are special cases' oversells a reformulation; there is no new guarantee (e.g., on representation quality, generalization, or avoidance of collapse) tied to the supervision.

Empirical gains are marginal and largely not statistically significant. Across Tables 2–3, improvements over the strongest baselines (GRACE, GAE, SGRL) are often within one standard deviation (e.g., hazard 0.650 vs 0.642 breast; 0.627 vs 0.625 lung vs GAE). The paper's own Bonferroni-corrected tests (Table 15) show significance only against GraphCL and SGRL on a subset of node-level tasks, never against GRACE — the closest competitor. The abstract's claim of 'consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines' is therefore stronger than the evidence warrants.

The central modeling choice — simulating knockdown by zeroing the target gene's node and edge features — is a crude feature perturbation, not a structural/topological perturbation, which sits awkwardly with the paper's framing about leveraging 'structural changes' from real perturbations. The relationship between the artificial view Ga and the teacher graph Ha (estimated from a different cell-line domain, with different network statistics per Table 8) is not analyzed; domain mismatch between LINCS teacher GRNs and TCGA patient GRNs is acknowledged only indirectly.

Statistical testing methodology is questionable: Student's t-test over 10-fold CV folds treats highly dependent fold-level metrics as independent samples, inflating or deflating significance unpredictably. No comparison against GRACE with any test is provided despite it being the natural ablation-like baseline.

The entire pipeline rests on estimated Bayesian-network GRNs; all methods, including w/o-pretrain, inherit estimation artifacts. While Appendix H examines filtering thresholds, the downstream conclusions could be sensitive to the specific GRN estimator (Imoto et al. 2002 / INGOR), and no alternative GRN-inference method is tested as a sensitivity check.

Missing domain-specific baselines: MuSe-GNN and other GRN-oriented self-supervised methods discussed in Related Work are not empirically compared, weakening the claim of state-of-the-art performance in this application domain. The ablation against GRACE is also muddied by an admitted non-identical loss definition.
No code or data-pipeline release is mentioned, which, combined with the heavy bespoke pipeline (supercomputer GRN estimation, LINCS preprocessing, Optuna tuning), limits reproducibility in practice.

Minor presentation issues reduce polish: inconsistent use of ϕ for both reference and learned models, the 'contractive learning' typo, and a confusing passage where pϕ/p notation shifts meaning across Sections 3–4 and Appendix A.

Subtype labels (PAM50) are computed from the same expression data that generates node features, a potential circularity for the subtype task; this affects all methods equally but is not discussed, and absolute subtype performance (0.85 accuracy, NMI ≤ 0.18) suggests the task itself is weakly learnable from GRN embeddings.
